name: Daria Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Daria, thanks for fitting me in. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential, so you can tell me your public view and your private one. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sam and I have a small mixed place called Willow Bank, twenty hectares. We milk sixty goats, make cheese in a little dairy room we built three years ago, and there's an old apple orchard and a market garden for salad and squash. A normal day is milking at six, then cheese-making till noon, then the garden or the orchard, and Saturdays I'm at the farmers' market in town. I love the cheese, it's like cooking for a living, and what wears me out is that I'm doing four jobs and paying off a loan for the dairy room.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said four jobs. Where does AI fit in, if it does?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day, honestly. I use an AI assistant to write the product descriptions for our web shop, to keep track of milk yields per goat, and to plan the garden rotation. Last month it spotted that one goat's yield had dropped two days before I noticed she was lame. Money's tight, we've maybe two weeks of bills in the bank because everything goes on the loan, but the tools are cheap and they save me hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: We'll go through five pictures of the future, one at a time. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still worth using, it saves me time every week. Online I'd probably say people expected too much too soon. At the market I'd just say I like the tools and move on to selling cheese.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine. The tools I use now are already a big help, and if they stop getting better, I'll still use them. My worries are the loan, the weather and keeping customers coming back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as I am. I'd keep using the AI for the web shop and records, maybe try a new tool for the accounts. Nothing big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly disappointed, but life's full anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So for you, what you've got now is roughly the ceiling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much. It already writes better cheese descriptions than I do, it just can't taste the cheese. So I'd still be the one who decides what's good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be focused on instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paying off the dairy room loan by 2029 and building up the online orders. If the online shop doubled, we'd be comfortable for the first time. That's my real target.

S0.say: I'd say it's still worth using because it saves me time every week, and people expected too much too soon. At the market I'd just get back to selling cheese.
S0.think: For me it's fine, because the tools I use already help a lot. My real worries are the loan, the weather and keeping customers.
S0.do: Keeps using AI for the web shop and records and may try a new tool for accounts. Focuses on paying off the dairy room loan by 2029 and growing online orders.
S0.quote: It already writes better cheese descriptions than I do, it just can't taste the cheese.
S0.fieldNote: Daria is already a daily AI user and gets real value from it, like spotting a lame goat early. She'd be mildly disappointed by a plateau but not changed. Her focus is the dairy room loan and building online sales.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now with more change. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's an opportunity for small farms if they're quick. The ones who use the tools will do fine. I'd post that in the small farmers' group and get a mix of thumbs up and angry faces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think this is good for us. We're small enough to change quickly, and a couple of robots could take the hard work off us. My worry is whether customers keep buying fancy cheese if their own jobs are wobbling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd look at leasing a robot weeder for the market garden, there are already ones that run on solar. I'd use AI for marketing more, maybe start farm visits with cheese tastings. And I'd try a milking system for the goats if a lease made sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly, even a bit excited. A small worry about customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a robot actually do on Willow Bank?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Weeding, mostly. I spend twelve hours a week on my knees pulling weeds, and I'd give that job to a robot tomorrow and not miss it once. Maybe milking, later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for it with two weeks of money in the bank?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lease, not buy. I'd look for a scheme where you pay monthly and hand it back if it's no good. I'd never take a second loan, Sam would leave me.

S1.say: I'd say it's an opportunity for small farms if they're quick, and those who use the tools will do fine. I'd post it in the small farmers' group.
S1.think: I think this is good for us because we're small and can change fast. I'd worry whether customers keep buying fancy cheese if their own jobs wobble.
S1.do: Looks into leasing a solar robot weeder in the first year and a milking system if a lease makes sense. Uses AI more for marketing and starts farm visits with cheese tastings.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, with a small worry about customers.
S1.quote: I spend twelve hours a week on my knees pulling weeds, and I'd give that job to a robot tomorrow and not miss it once.
S1.fieldNote: Daria sees steady change as a chance to drop the hardest work. She is careful with money, leasing rather than borrowing again. Her worry about customers' spending is sharp and shows she thinks about demand, not just her own tasks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next one is very fast. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt quickly, there's no other choice. I'd tell people at the market to look for what robots can't do. Online I'd say governments need to help people get through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the farm itself is fine, I can bring in robots. What worries me is whether anyone can afford handmade goat's cheese when their jobs vanish. Two years is too short for customers to settle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put everything into what makes us different: the story, the visits, the farm stays. I'd lease robots for the hard jobs within months, to cut costs. And I'd cut our own spending to nothing extra, because the loan doesn't stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can see what to do, but the money's thin and the time's short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You talked about customers. What happens to the cheese?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot can make cheese, but it can't make a Saturday morning at the market feel like a Saturday morning. I'd bet on that. Some people will pay for a person behind the cheese, I hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the cheese doesn't sell, what's the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sell the goats, keep the orchard, and rent out the dairy room. That's the worst case. And I'd talk to the bank before the loan payment is missed.

S2.say: I'd say adapt quickly because there's no other choice, and look for what robots can't do. Online I'd say governments need to help people through it.
S2.think: The farm is fine because I can bring in robots. The worry is whether anyone can afford handmade goat's cheese when their jobs vanish.
S2.do: Leases robots for the hard jobs within months and focuses the business on farm stays, visits and the story behind the cheese. Cuts household spending and talks to the bank early about the loan.
S2.feel: Anxious, seeing what to do but short of money and time.
S2.quote: A robot can make cheese, but it can't make a Saturday morning at the market feel like a Saturday morning.
S2.fieldNote: Daria isn't worried about being replaced; she's worried about her customers losing income. Her bet on the human experience of the market is hopeful and she admits it. She has a clear worst-case plan of selling the goats and renting the dairy room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same, with more time. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say plan now, five years is enough time if you start this year. I'd post about the robots we try, good and bad, so other small farms can learn. Being honest about what works is useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough for me to clear the loan and set the farm up for robots. I'd be sixty-three, and if it works, Sam and I can step back a bit. It's a race, but a fair one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd overpay the loan to clear it by 2029, then lease robots as soon as they're good enough, and add farm stays in the old barn. I'd use AI to run the bookings and the web shop. And I'd put away whatever the farm stays bring in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. There's a worry in the background, but I'd be busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, what would you do now that you wouldn't with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but fewer. Thirty goats with names is a farm, sixty goats with numbers is a factory, and the robots will win the factory. We'd keep the ones with names.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still keep the goats?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Plus the orchard, the garden and the barn. Spread it around, so no single thing sinks us.

S3.say: I'd say plan now, because five years is enough if you start this year. I'd post honestly about the robots we try so other small farms can learn.
S3.think: Five years is enough to clear the loan and set the farm up for robots. If it works, Sam and I can step back a bit at sixty-three.
S3.do: Overpays the loan to clear it by 2029, then leases robots once they're good enough and adds farm stays in the barn. Uses AI to run bookings and saves the farm stay income.
S3.feel: Uneasy in the background but busy and focused.
S3.quote: Thirty goats with names is a farm, sixty goats with numbers is a factory, and the robots will win the factory.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years let Daria clear her debt before she invests, which she cares about. She plans to halve the herd and compete on character, not volume. Her idea of posting honestly about trials shows a practical, community-minded streak.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so use it. I'd encourage people to try things now. That's what I'd say online and at the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For us, it's mostly good. Ten years is enough to adapt the farm and retire on our own terms. I think we'd be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Clear the loan, try robots one at a time as they prove themselves, and build the farm stays. I'd train a younger person from the village in cheese-making, so the farm has a future. And I'd keep using AI every day, like now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Interested, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do you see Willow Bank in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots doing the weeding, a young woman doing the cheese, and me showing tourists the goats and talking too much. That's my picture, anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Customers again, a bit. If people don't have work, who has money for cheese and farm stays? But ten years gives the country time to figure that out, I hope.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift, so use it and try things now. I'd say it online and at the market.
S4.think: For us it's mostly good, because ten years is enough to adapt the farm and retire on our own terms. I think we'd be fine.
S4.do: Clears the loan, tries robots one at a time as they prove themselves and builds up farm stays. Trains a young person from the village in cheese-making and keeps using AI daily.
S4.quote: Robots doing the weeding, a young woman doing the cheese, and me showing tourists the goats and talking too much.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Daria is relaxed and even pictures a happy handover. Her lingering worry is still about customers' spending power. She thinks in steps and leases, not leaps, despite being an early adopter.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because of the customers, not the robots. I can automate the goats, but I can't automate people having money to spend. What would help is cheap leasing for small farm robots and something that keeps money in people's pockets while things settle.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Who owns the robots. If they're all leased from big companies, we're just renting our own farms back. I'd like small farms to be able to own them outright one day.

headlineQuote: I can automate the goats, but I can't automate people having money to spend.
portrait: Daria Chen is a 58-year-old smallholder who milks sixty goats, makes cheese and grows fruit and vegetables with her partner Sam. She's paying off a loan for her dairy room and has about two weeks of savings. She uses AI every day for her web shop, records and planning, and she'd happily give the weeding to a robot. She's practical and in the middle politically. She stays calm in slower scenarios, gets anxious about fast AGI mainly because her customers might stop buying, and with more time plans to clear the loan, lease robots and add farm stays.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because customers could lose their jobs and stop buying handmade cheese before things settle.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap leasing of robots for small farms and something that keeps money in people's pockets during the change.
